subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: In the Delhi flat, Parveen practised her reading for the class quiz while her brother Ujjwal sat nearby with his cricket cards. She read, “The river is very long?” with her voice going up at the end. Ujjwal frowned. “Are you not sure?” She shook her head, surprised. “No, I am sure. I just say it like that when I'm being polite.” Ujjwal laughed. “Then everyone will think you don't know.” She tried again with her voice going down on “long,” and it sounded firm. “Oh, so it can be either,” he said, “you have to look at the rest of her face too.”

qa.q: What was Parveen practising for?
qa.a: The class quiz.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal think Parveen was unsure?
qa.a: Her voice went up at the end of the sentence like a question, which he read as doubt, though she said it was her polite way of speaking.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next time he hears a rising voice?
qa.a: He could ask whether she is unsure and look at the rest of the situation before deciding it means doubt.

qa.q: How might Parveen's teacher hear the rising voice in the quiz?
qa.a: The teacher could take it for doubt and mark her as unsure, even if Parveen knows the answer.

grounding: A rising pitch may signal a question or uncertainty, but Parveen shows it can also be politeness, so context matters.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: “Say it again, Kalyani,” said Arnab, tapping the table. “Ten past five?” Her voice climbed on the last word. “Are you asking me or telling me?” he said. “Telling you, silly!” Kalyani said, tilting her head. “In our village everyone talks that way. It goes up when we're being nice.” Arnab thought about it. “In my class if it goes up, the teacher says you're guessing.” “Well, I'm not guessing.” She said it again, falling on “five.” “See? Ten past five. Same words.” Arnab grinned. “Fine. Next time I'll ask before I decide you're unsure.”

qa.q: What time did Kalyani say?
qa.a: Ten past five.

qa.q: Why did Arnab ask if Kalyani was asking or telling?
qa.a: He heard her voice rise on the last word and wondered if she was unsure, since his teacher treats a rising voice as guessing.

qa.q: What did Arnab decide to do differently?
qa.a: He decided to ask before assuming Kalyani is unsure, because a rising voice can be a regional habit and not doubt.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when her friends read her habit as guessing?
qa.a: She might feel misunderstood or annoyed, since to her the rising voice is just politeness from home. 😅

grounding: A rising tone can mean a question or doubt, but for Kalyani it is politeness and a regional habit.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Pooja. When Bidisha joined our class from Sydney, I thought she was the most unsure person I'd ever met. Everything she said went up at the end. “I live near the temple? My dad's a nurse? I like drawing?” I kept answering, “Yes? Okay?” as if she'd asked me something. Once she said, “The answer is forty-two?” and I told her not to worry, it was probably right. She gave me a funny look. “I know it's right.” Later she explained that where she grew up, lots of people talk like that, even when they're sure. Now I listen to her face, not just the end of her sentences.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha join the class from?
qa.a: Bidisha joined from Sydney.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Pooja said the answer was probably right?
qa.a: Bidisha felt puzzled and perhaps a bit annoyed, since she was sure and the rising tone was just her way of speaking.

qa.q: What does Pooja do now, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Pooja listens to Bidisha's face as well as the tone, since a rising ending can be a habit rather than doubt.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had never learned about the habit?
qa.a: Pooja might keep treating Bidisha as unsure, which could feel patronising to someone who is actually confident.

grounding: Shows a child reading a rising voice as doubt, and learning it can be a regional speaking habit instead.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: Class note, Thursday. Minakshi, Class 5 science. Ankita answers almost everything with her voice going up at the end: “Chlorophyll? Sunlight?” For weeks I took this as doubt and kept giving her more hints. Today I asked her privately if she was unsure. She looked surprised. “No, Ma'am. At home we're told not to sound too sure in front of elders. It's rude.” That was new to me. Her answers are nearly always right. I explained that in class a falling voice simply says “this is my answer”, and it isn't rude. She tried it: “Chlorophyll.” Down at the end. She smiled. I've stopped giving her hints she doesn't need.

qa.q: What did Ankita's family teach about sounding sure?
qa.a: They taught her not to sound too sure in front of elders, because it's rude.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when Minakshi asked if she was unsure?
qa.a: Ankita felt surprised, since she was confident; the rising tone was politeness, not doubt.

qa.q: What did Minakshi change after the talk?
qa.a: Minakshi explained that a falling tone isn't rude in class and stopped giving Ankita hints she didn't need.

qa.q: How had Minakshi read the rising tone for weeks?
qa.a: Minakshi took it as doubt and kept offering hints, not knowing it was a politeness habit.

grounding: Shows a teacher reading a child's rising tone as doubt when it was politeness taught at home, and context changing the meaning.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: Wednesday. Nazia's diary. Ritu sent a voice note about the science fair: “I'll bring the batteries? And I'll come at eight?” Her voice went up at the end of everything. I didn't know if she was asking me or telling me. Is she even sure she's coming? I nearly asked Aapi to take me instead. Then I just called her. “Ritu, are you coming at eight or not?” She laughed. “Yes, definitely! I always sound like that on voice notes. My mum says I sound like I'm asking permission.” So I stopped worrying. She came at five to eight, with the batteries.

qa.q: What did Ritu say she would bring?
qa.a: Ritu said she would bring the batteries.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling after the voice note?
qa.a: Nazia felt uncertain and a little worried that Ritu might not be sure about coming.

qa.q: Why was calling Ritu a good idea?
qa.a: It checked the meaning directly, showing the rising tone was Ritu's usual habit, not doubt.

qa.q: How does Ritu's mother describe Ritu's voice notes?
qa.a: Ritu's mother says she sounds like she's asking permission, which shows the rising tone is a habit.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's rising tone as doubt, and checking to find it was a speaking habit.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage:
Vasudha's family had moved to the kasba from Mangaluru only a week ago. At Deepak's father's shop she read from her list: "One kilo rice? Half-kilo toor dal? And one soap?" Each item went up at the end like a question.

Deepak paused, scoop in hand. "Are you sure? You keep asking."
Vasudha blinked. "I'm not asking. I'm telling."
"But your voice goes up."
She laughed. "Everyone in my house talks like that. It's polite, sort of. When I really don't know, I say 'I think'."

Deepak weighed out the rice. Then Vasudha frowned at the list. "Wait. Was it two soaps?" This time her voice went up, and so did her eyebrows. Deepak grinned. "That one's a real question."

qa.q: Where had Vasudha's family moved from?
qa.a: From Mangaluru, only a week ago.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel when Vasudha's voice kept going up?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and unsure whether to trust the list, thinking she doubted her own order.

qa.q: How could Deepak tell Vasudha's real question from her usual way of talking?
qa.a: By the context: the frown, the raised eyebrows and the "Wait" came with the last one, showing genuine doubt.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Deepak asks "Are you sure?"
qa.a: She is surprised and a bit amused, since in her house a rising voice is simply polite, not doubtful.

grounding: It shows a child reading a rising voice as doubt and learning it can be a polite or regional habit, with context showing a real question.
